passages.text: The clock on the wall had stopped at twenty past three. Nadia shifted in the plastic chair, her coat folded neatly across her lap despite the heat. She had arrived before the receptionist, before the strip lights had flickered on, and now the room was filling with people who did not look at each other. A child tugged at his mother’s sleeve. The woman beside Nadia turned the pages of a magazine without reading them. When the double doors finally swung open, Nadia stood so quickly that her coat slipped to the floor, and she left it there.
passages.label: Extract A — The Waiting Room

passages.text: Frank pressed the fork into the soil and felt it give. The earth here was dark and heavy from last night’s rain, nothing like the chalky ground at the front of the house where nothing grew. He had been coming to the allotment every morning since March, long before the seeds had any reason to show themselves, and each time he unlocked the gate he noticed something: a shoot, a weed, the first white roots of the potatoes curling below the surface. His neighbour, Delyth, waved from three plots down. She was already harvesting courgettes the size of her forearm. Frank looked at his own neat rows and said nothing.
passages.label: Extract B — The Allotment

passages.text: The beam swept the water every eight seconds. Seren counted it from the kitchen window, pressing her forehead against the cold glass until it misted around her face. Her father’s boat had left the harbour at four o’clock, when the sky was still pale and the gulls were quiet. That was nine hours ago. Her mother moved between the stove and the table, laying out bread, cheese, a pot of tea — more food than two people could eat. Neither of them mentioned the forecast. The radio on the shelf crackled with static, and Seren reached across to turn it off, then changed her mind.
passages.label: Extract C — The Lighthouse

method_card.title: Explicit and Implicit Information
method_card.content: Every fiction text contains information on two levels. Explicit information is stated directly — you can point to it in the text. Implicit information is suggested through word choice, description, and detail — you have to read between the lines.

passages.text: The stalls were crammed together like teeth in an overcrowded mouth. Mangoes sat in bright pyramids, their skins blushing from green to gold, and the fishmonger’s ice glittered under a strip of bare bulbs. Kemi moved between the aisles with her elbows tucked in, pressed forward by the crowd behind her. The air was thick with chilli smoke and the sweet rot of overripe fruit. Someone was frying plantain nearby — the oil crackled and spat. She kept one hand on her purse and the other reaching forward, parting the bodies ahead of her like curtains.
passages.label: Extract A — The Market

passages.text: By morning the garden had been remade. Every blade of grass wore a sleeve of white, and the washing line sagged under a weight it was never built to carry. Isobel pressed her palm flat against the back door and pulled it away to find her handprint preserved in condensation, five fingers splayed like a fossil in stone. The cold had a taste — metallic, clean, the opposite of everything inside the house. She stepped out in her mother’s boots, two sizes too large, and the frost crunched beneath her like broken china. Nothing moved. Even the robin on the fence post looked painted there.
passages.label: Extract B — The Frost

passages.text: They had stripped the building to its skeleton. Where corridors once funnelled laughter and the squeak of trainers on linoleum, there was only air and the memory of walls. Rafiq stood in what had been the main hall and looked up through three floors of nothing to a rectangle of grey sky. Dust sifted down like slow rain. The remaining beams jutted out at angles, broken ribs of a body that refused to fall neatly. Somewhere a pipe dripped into standing water, each drop arriving with the patience of a clock that had outlived its building. He could still smell the paint they had used to cover the damp — institution green, the colour of waiting.
passages.label: Extract C — The Demolition

summaryParts.text: The metaphor of the building as a body with “broken ribs” personifies the structure as something that has been hurt, not just demolished.
The simile “like slow rain” suggests the dust falls violently and dangerously.
summaryParts.explain: The word “slow” creates the opposite effect — the dust drifts gently and quietly. The simile emphasises the eerie calm of the demolition site, not danger.

summaryParts.text: The phrase “the patience of a clock” personifies the dripping water as something that persists through time.
The colour “institution green” is used to suggest the building was cheerful and well-maintained.
summaryParts.explain: “Institution green” connotes public buildings, bureaucracy, neglect. Combined with “the colour of waiting,” it suggests endurance and tedium, not cheer.

summaryParts.text: The contrast between past sounds (“laughter,” “squeak of trainers”) and present emptiness heightens the sense of loss.

gold.context: A good response evaluates how the body metaphor (“skeleton,” “broken ribs,” “refused to fall neatly”) makes the building seem almost alive and suffering. passages.text: Priya ran. Her feet slapped the wet pavement, each stride jolting through her knees, her hips, her ribs. Behind her, the footsteps matched her pace — not gaining, not falling back, just there. She turned left without thinking, cutting down an alley she half-remembered from childhood, where the walls were close enough to touch with both hands. The bins. The broken glass. The smell of something rotting. She didn’t slow down. At the end of the alley was a gate, and beyond the gate was the park, and beyond the park was the road, and beyond the road was home. She reached for the latch. It didn’t move.
passages.label: Extract A — The Chase

passages.text: Marcus had rehearsed his opening line fourteen times on the bus. He had timed it, trimmed it, practised the pause before the second clause. But now, sitting in the leather chair that was slightly too low, facing a woman whose glasses reflected the overhead light so that he could not see her eyes, he found that every prepared word had dissolved like sugar in hot water, leaving nothing behind but a faint sweetness he could not quite name. She asked him to begin. He opened his mouth. The room waited. What came out was not what he had practised. It was better.
passages.label: Extract B — The Interview

passages.text: The sea came in. It came in slowly, as it always did on this stretch of coast, creeping across the flat sand in thin sheets that caught the light and turned it into something living, something that breathed and retreated and breathed again, so that a person standing at the water’s edge might believe the tide would never actually reach them. But it would. Angharad knew this because she had watched it every evening for eleven months, standing in the same spot with her shoes in her hand and the wind pulling her hair sideways, and each time the water arrived at exactly the place she was standing, as though it had been looking for her. Tonight she did not step back.
passages.label: Extract C — The Tide

passages.text: Dr Osei’s waiting room smelled of floor polish and old magazines. Tariq sat in the corner, watching the second hand of the wall clock move in tiny jerks. His mother was filling in a form, pressing hard with the pen as though the paper might resist. He counted the ceiling tiles. Twelve across, nine down. One hundred and eight tiles. He had been counting things all week: steps to school, cracks in the pavement, the number of times his father cleared his throat before speaking. When the receptionist called his name, Tariq stood up and walked through the door. The room on the other side was smaller than he had expected, and warmer, and Dr Osei was already smiling. He sat down. He did not count the tiles.
passages.label: Extract A — The Appointment

passages.text: The key had been in the drawer since before Eleri was born. Her grandmother had told her this once, casually, while peeling apples at the kitchen table, and then never mentioned it again. It was brass, heavy, with teeth too large for any lock in the house. Eleri had tried every door, every cupboard, even the padlock on the garden shed. Nothing fit. Now, twenty years later, she was standing in the hallway of her grandmother’s empty house, holding the key in one hand and a letter in the other. The letter said only: the blue door at the end of the garden. There had never been a blue door at the end of the garden. But when Eleri walked through the kitchen and looked out through the window, there it was — blue paint, peeling, a lock at exactly the right height.
passages.label: Extract B — The Key

passages.text: In the morning the orchard was full of light. The trees stood in their rows like something patient, their branches heavy with fruit that nobody had picked, and the grass between them was long enough to hide in. Dafydd walked between the rows with his hands in his pockets, touching nothing. He had come back for the funeral but stayed for this — the quiet, the warmth, the way the light moved through the leaves as though searching for something it had lost. His mother had planted these trees the year he was born, pressing each sapling into the ground with her bare hands while his father held him on the porch. That was the story, anyway. Now the house was sold and the new owners wanted the orchard cleared for a patio. Dafydd reached up and picked a single apple. He bit into it. It tasted of nothing he could name and everything he could remember.
passages.label: Extract C — The Orchard

Analysing structure means explaining how the writer organises the text and why those choices affect the reader.

passages.text: From the stands, the track was a strip of red between two lines of white. The crowd was loud, flags and hands and voices all moving at once. Then the gun cracked and the runners burst forward. Ayo was in lane three. She could not hear the crowd anymore. All she could hear was her own breathing, hard and fast, and the slap of her spikes against the rubber. The girl in lane four was pulling ahead. Ayo’s lungs burned. She leaned forward and found something she did not know she had. In the stands, her father had stopped clapping and was simply watching, his hands frozen in front of his chest, his mouth slightly open.
passages.label: Extract A — The Sports Day

passages.text: The photograph had been taken in 1974. Nasreen could tell from the colour — that washed-out orange that old film stock turns to, as though time itself were a kind of stain. Three women stood in front of a bus stop, squinting into the sun. The woman on the left was her grandmother, though Nasreen would never have recognised her without being told. She looked young, careless, her hair blown sideways by a wind that had stopped blowing fifty years ago. Nasreen turned the photograph over. On the back, in pencil so faint it was almost gone: Lahore, March. We leave tomorrow. She turned it back. Her grandmother’s face was still smiling. She had no idea what was coming.
passages.label: Extract B — The Photograph

passages.text: The first lightning strike hit the ridge at quarter past two. From the village below it looked like a crack in the sky, white and sudden and wrong, as though the air itself had broken. In the schoolhouse, the children pressed their faces to the glass and counted the seconds between flash and thunder. Miss Parry told them to sit down. On the ridge, Gethin crouched behind a wall that was no longer keeping anything out. Rain came at him sideways, filling his eyes, his mouth, the space between his collar and his neck. He could not see the village. He could not see anything except the grass flattened by wind and the shape of his own hands. Below him, in the warm schoolhouse, his daughter was counting. One, two, three, four. She did not know the ridge was where her father worked.
passages.label: Extract C — The Storm

method_card.title: Structural Analysis: Focus and Perspective Shifts
method_card.content: Writers control what the reader focuses on and whose perspective they experience. Shifts in focus (wide to narrow, external to internal, present to past) and perspective (one character to another, or from action to thought) are deliberate structural choices that shape meaning and reader engagement.

summaryParts.text: The writer alternates between two locations — the schoolhouse and the ridge — to create a structural parallel between father and daughter.

summaryParts.explain: The wall is described as “no longer keeping anything out” — it offers no protection. The shift to Gethin increases tension by showing how exposed and vulnerable he is.

summaryParts.text: The daughter counting seconds structurally mirrors the opening’s description of the lightning, connecting her innocently to her father’s danger without her knowing it.
The final sentence creates dramatic irony: the daughter does not know her father is on the ridge, but the reader does.

summaryParts.explain: The scenes are deeply connected — father and daughter are linked by the storm. The structural juxtaposition between the warm schoolhouse and the exposed ridge intensifies both settings through contrast.

gold.context: A good response evaluates how the dual perspective creates dramatic irony and emotional tension that a single viewpoint could not achieve. The alternation forces the reader to hold both realities simultaneously. Should consider the structural impact of the final sentence revealing the family connection.

gold.context: A good response identifies that counting appears in both locations: the children count seconds between flash and thunder, and the daughter counts at the end (“One, two, three, four”). passages.text: The steps went down further than Megan expected. Each one was narrower than the last, and the wall beside her was damp under her fingertips. She should have brought a torch. The light from the kitchen doorway above had shrunk to a bright rectangle no bigger than a playing card. Something dripped in the darkness below — a slow, patient sound, like a tap left running in an empty house. The air changed halfway down: colder, thicker, carrying a smell she could not place. Old stone. Old water. Something else. She reached the bottom step and her foot found not solid ground but an inch of standing water, shockingly cold. She stood still. Somewhere ahead, in the darkness she could not see into, something moved.
passages.label: Extract A — The Cellar

passages.text: Jermaine had not seen his brother in four years. He had rehearsed this moment so many times that the real version felt like a copy of something better. Dylan was thinner. His hair was longer. He stood in the doorway of the flat with his hands in his jacket pockets, smiling a smile that did not quite reach his eyes. They did not hug. Jermaine said “come in” and Dylan said “cheers” and they sat on opposite ends of the sofa like strangers on a bus. The television was on. Neither of them watched it. Jermaine made tea and brought it through on a tray their mother had given him, and when he set it down he noticed his hands were shaking. Dylan noticed too. Neither of them said anything. The tea cooled between them like a question nobody wanted to ask.
passages.label: Extract B — The Reunion

passages.text: The rock face was not beautiful. Catrin had read descriptions of mountains that made them sound like cathedrals or sleeping gods, but this was just rock — grey, wet, indifferent to her presence. She wedged her fingers into a crack and pulled, and the crack held, and she moved up six inches. That was how it went. Crack, pull, six inches. Below her the valley had disappeared into cloud, which meant she could not see how far she would fall. This was, she supposed, a mercy. Her arms ached in a way that had passed through pain and arrived somewhere duller, somewhere that felt permanent. She had been climbing for three hours and the summit was still above her, hidden behind a curve of stone that might reveal another curve of stone behind it. There was no one to hear her if she shouted. There was no reason to shout. She reached for the next crack and pulled.
passages.label: Extract C — The Climb

steps.label: Step 1
steps.content: Start by taking a position. In this case, there is strong evidence to agree: the writer uses darkness, unknown sounds, and a final mysterious movement to build fear.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.content: Look at the evidence. The dripping is given a simile — “like a tap left running in an empty house.” The word “patient” personifies the sound, as though it has been waiting for Megan. This makes the ordinary sound feel threatening.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.content: The ending — “something moved” — is deliberately vague. The writer does not tell us what moved. This forces the reader to imagine, which is often more frightening than knowing.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: I strongly agree. The writer creates fear through sensory detail (the cold water, the changing air), the personification of the drip as “patient,” and the terrifying vagueness of “something moved.” The cellar becomes frightening not through what is shown but through what is withheld — the reader’s imagination fills the darkness with threat.

worked_examples.question: A student said: “The writer makes the cellar feel genuinely frightening.” To what extent do you agree?

steps.label: Step 1
steps.content: There is overwhelming evidence to agree. The writer shows distance through physical positioning, minimal dialogue, and avoidance of emotional expression.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.content: The simile “like strangers on a bus” is devastating because these are brothers, not strangers. The comparison highlights how far apart they have become.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.content: However, the distance is complicated. Jermaine’s shaking hands reveal that he does feel something — the emotional distance is performed, not felt. The brothers are pretending to be distant because they don’t know how to be close after four years.

steps.label: Step 4
steps.content: The final image — tea cooling between them “like a question nobody wanted to ask” — confirms this. The question exists; they just cannot voice it.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: I agree that the writer creates emotional distance, but would argue it is a performed distance that masks deeper feeling. The brothers sit apart, avoid eye contact, and speak in monosyllables, but the shaking hands and the metaphor of the cooling tea reveal suppressed emotion. The writer’s achievement is showing distance and connection simultaneously — the brothers are close enough to hurt, which is why they sit so far apart.

passages.text:
EXTRACT 1:
The storm arrived without warning. One moment the sky was clear; the next, the rain came down in sheets so thick that Leila could not see the end of the garden. Thunder cracked directly overhead, sharp and sudden, like a whip against stone. She pressed her back to the kitchen wall and counted. She had been told that counting the gap between lightning and thunder would tell you how far away the storm was, but this storm was not far away. This storm was here.

---

EXTRACT 2:
Grant had been waiting for the storm all afternoon. He stood on the back step with his arms folded, watching the clouds build above the hills like a slow bruise spreading across skin. When the first drops fell, he tilted his face upward and let them hit him. The thunder, when it came, rolled across the valley in long, low waves that he felt in his chest before he heard them in his ears. He did not move. The rain soaked through his shirt. He stayed.
passages.label: Extract A — Two descriptions of a storm

passages.text:
EXTRACT 1:
The village appeared around a bend in the road as though it had been hiding. Rosalind slowed the car and leaned forward over the wheel. The houses were small and grey, pressed together along a single street that ended at a harbour wall. Fishing boats sat at odd angles on the mud, their paint peeling, their ropes trailing in the water. Nothing moved. A gull stood on a chimney pot and watched her drive past. She parked outside the only shop and sat for a moment with the engine off, listening to the silence. It was not a welcoming silence. It was the silence of a place that had already decided what it thought of her.

---

EXTRACT 2:
Omar smelled the city before he saw it. Diesel and cardamom and hot tarmac, all of it carried through the open window of the bus as they descended the hill. Then the buildings rose around them — concrete towers with balconies draped in laundry, shop fronts spilling goods onto the pavement, a man selling watermelons from the back of a truck. The noise hit him next: horns, music, a voice calling prices through a loudspeaker. Omar pressed his face to the glass. Everything was moving. Everything was alive. He wanted to get off the bus and walk into it.
passages.label: Extract B — Two descriptions of arriving somewhere new

passages.text:
EXTRACT 1:
Sioned cleared her mother’s house in three days. She worked methodically, room by room, filling black bags with clothes that still smelled of lavender and placing books into boxes she had labelled with a marker pen. She did not sit on the bed. She did not open the curtains. On the last afternoon, she found a shopping list on the kitchen counter in her mother’s handwriting — milk, bread, the good marmalade — and she folded it once and put it in her coat pocket. She locked the front door and posted the key through the letterbox and walked to the car without looking back.

---

EXTRACT 2:
After his father died, Kwame could not stop touching things. The bannister his father had gripped every morning. The armchair whose cushion still held the shape of his body. The kitchen tap that dripped because his father had always meant to fix it and never had. Kwame turned it off and then turned it on again, letting it drip. He sat in the armchair and felt the cushion slowly reshape itself around him, and he did not know whether he was preserving something or erasing it. He stayed in the house for a week. He did not clear anything. He was not ready for the objects to forget.
passages.label: Extract C — Two descriptions of loss

method_card.title: Comparing Writers’ Methods
method_card.content: Comparison means analysing how two writers approach a similar subject using different methods. Focus on technique, not just content. Don’t just say what each writer describes — explain how they describe it and why their approaches differ in effect.

gold.context: A good response identifies the core methodological contrast: Sioned processes grief through action and control (clearing the house methodically, not sitting on the bed, not looking back) while Kwame processes grief through touch and preservation (touching the bannister, sitting in the armchair, letting the tap drip). Should analyse how the writers use objects differently: for Sioned, objects are packed away; for Kwame, objects are touched and preserved. The shopping list vs the dripping tap are key contrasts.

summaryParts.text: Both writers explore grief through a character’s physical actions in the home of a dead parent, but their methods create opposite effects.
Sioned is presented as emotionless because she clears the house efficiently without crying.
summaryParts.explain: Efficiency is not emotionlessness. The details she avoids (not sitting on the bed, not opening curtains) and the item she keeps (the shopping list) reveal deep feeling beneath the controlled surface. The writer shows grief through restraint, not its absence.

summaryParts.text: Kwame’s grief is shown through compulsive touching — he cannot let go of the physical traces of his father.
The shopping list and the dripping tap serve similar functions: both are small, ordinary details that carry enormous emotional weight because they preserve the dead person’s presence.
Extract 1 is better because Sioned is stronger and braver than Kwame.

passages.text: The river was wider than Asha remembered. She stood at the edge where the bank crumbled into brown water and watched a plastic bottle turn slowly in the current. It was March, and the trees on the far side were still bare, their branches scratching at a sky the colour of old newspaper. Her brother Ravi was already in the boat, a flat-bottomed punt he had borrowed from the farm. He held the pole loosely, one end trailing in the water, and said nothing. The boat was not built for two people and their belongings. They had a suitcase, a bin bag of clothes, and a cardboard box sealed with brown tape that their mother had pressed into Asha’s hands that morning without explaining what was inside. Asha climbed in. The boat dipped and water sloshed over the side, soaking the box. Ravi pushed off from the bank. The current took them immediately, pulling them sideways, and the far bank, which had looked close, suddenly looked very far away.
passages.label: Extract A — The Crossing

passages.text: The hall smelled of floor wax and adrenaline. Seventy-two desks had been arranged in rows of eight, each one bearing a number card, two sharpened pencils, and a glass of water nobody would drink. Yusuf found his seat — number forty-seven — and sat down. The chair was cold. Around him, the other competitors opened and closed their hands, rolled their necks, stared at the ceiling. One girl in the front row was whispering to herself with her eyes shut, her lips moving fast as though reciting a prayer or a formula. The invigilator walked to the front. She was small and precise, and when she spoke her voice carried without effort to every corner of the room. She told them they had ninety minutes. She told them to turn over their papers. Yusuf turned his over. The first question was one he had never seen before. It was beautiful. He picked up his pencil and felt something shift in his chest — not fear, but its opposite: the excitement of being exactly where he was supposed to be.
passages.label: Extract B — The Competition

passages.text: Beca had not been home in eleven years. She recognised the house by its gate — green paint, rusted hinge, the same gap at the bottom where next door’s cat used to squeeze through. The cat would be dead by now. She pushed the gate open and it made the sound she remembered, a low groan like a question being asked for the thousandth time. The garden was smaller. That was the first thing. The lawn that had been a football pitch and an ocean and a wilderness was now six paces from fence to fence. The apple tree that had held her rope swing was still there, but its trunk had split in a storm and someone had bolted the two halves together with a metal brace. It looked like it was being held together by force of will. Inside, the hallway still smelled of the same wood polish, as though the house had been holding its breath. Her old bedroom was a study now. Where her posters had been, there were bookshelves. Where her bed had stood, a desk faced the window. She looked through the window at the garden she had just crossed and realised she had spent her whole childhood in a space no larger than a car park. It had felt infinite.
passages.label: Extract C — The Return

Q1 (4 marks, ~5 mins): multiple choice — shade the four true statements. Explicit information only.
Q2 (8 marks, ~10 mins): analyse language. Quote specific words and explain effects.
Q3 (8 marks, ~10 mins): analyse how the structure creates the named effect — beginnings, endings, focus shifts.
Q4 (20 marks, ~20 mins): evaluate. Take a position, use evidence, analyse techniques.
method_card.title: Exam Skills: Paper 1 Reading Walkthrough
method_card.content: The Paper 1 Reading section has four questions on a single fiction extract. Each tests a different skill: finding information, analysing language, analysing structure, and evaluating. This lesson practises all four skills together, building exam stamina and helping you manage time and technique across the whole paper.

prerequisites.title: Structural Analysis: Focus and Perspective Shifts

exam_context.paper: Paper 1: Explorations in Creative Reading and Writing

gold.context: A good response analyses key language choices: the gate’s sound as “a low groan like a question being asked for the thousandth time” (personification + simile suggesting familiarity and weariness), the apple tree “held together by force of will” (personification suggesting fragile persistence), “the house had been holding its breath” (personification suggesting the house has been waiting for her). Should discuss how the language animates the house and garden, making them feel like living things that have aged alongside Beca.
gold.question: [Q2 skill] How does the writer use language to present Beca’s experience of returning home? Analyse the effects of specific words and phrases.

gold.context: A good response traces the structural journey: outside (gate, garden) → inside (hallway, bedroom) → looking back out (window to garden). This circular movement structurally mirrors Beca revisiting and reassessing her past. The key structural technique is the contrast between childhood perception (“a football pitch and an ocean and a wilderness”) and adult reality (“six paces from fence to fence”, “no larger than a car park”). The ending’s shift from present observation to past memory (“It had felt infinite”) is the emotional climax.
gold.question: [Q3 skill] How does the writer structure this passage to build towards the final realisation? Analyse the structural choices.

claims: Personification gives the house and garden human qualities
Contrast between childhood memory and adult reality creates poignancy
Structural detail foreshadows themes of loss and change
The ending collapses past and present into a single powerful insight

quotes.text: the house had been holding its breath
The lawn that had been a football pitch and an ocean and a wilderness was now six paces from fence to fence.
its trunk had split in a storm and someone had bolted the two halves together with a metal brace
she had spent her whole childhood in a space no larger than a car park. It had felt infinite.
Where her posters had been, there were bookshelves.

gold.question: Match each analytical point to its best supporting evidence.

gold.context: A good response evaluates how multiple techniques work together: personification (the house “holding its breath”), contrast (childhood imagination vs adult measurement), symbolism (the bolted apple tree), structural movement (outside → inside → looking back out). The final lines are the strongest evidence: the car park comparison deflates the childhood “wilderness” to something mundane, yet “It had felt infinite” redeems the memory. Should evaluate whether this tension between reality and memory is effective.
gold.question: [Q4 skill] A student said: “The writer powerfully conveys how returning home forces Beca to see her childhood differently.” To what extent do you agree? Evaluate, referring to specific techniques across the whole passage.
This full-paper analysis contains some strong and some flawed points. Click on the flawed ones.

summaryParts.text: The writer personifies the house and garden throughout, giving them human qualities (“holding its breath,” “force of will”) to suggest they have been waiting for Beca’s return.
The apple tree with its metal brace symbolises something damaged but surviving, perhaps mirroring Beca’s own relationship with home.
The passage is structured as a simple tour of the house with no deeper meaning beyond describing what Beca sees.
summaryParts.explain: The structure is deliberately designed: moving from outside to inside to looking back out creates a circular journey that mirrors Beca’s emotional reassessment. The final look through the window at the garden she just crossed is a structural choice that forces the childhood/adult comparison.

summaryParts.text: The final contrast between “a car park” and “infinite” is devastating because it captures how adulthood can diminish what childhood magnified.
The passage would be more effective if the writer directly stated that Beca was sad about returning home.
summaryParts.explain: The writer’s restraint is the technique. Beca’s feelings are shown through observation (the shrinking garden, the changed bedroom, the bolted tree) rather than stated. This indirect method is more powerful because it trusts the reader to feel the emotion.

silver.question: [Q3 skill] Match each structural observation to its supporting evidence.
[Q2 skill] Read this language analysis. Click on the parts that are weak or inaccurate.

summaryParts.text: The phrase “floor wax and adrenaline” combines a physical smell with an abstract concept, making the tension feel tangible and present.
The writer uses numbers like “seventy-two” and “rows of eight” to show the hall is boring and unimportant.
summaryParts.explain: The precise numbers create a sense of rigid order and formality, not boredom. They establish the clinical, high-stakes atmosphere of the competition.

summaryParts.text: The girl “whispering to herself with her eyes shut” is an effective detail that conveys nervous preparation through physical action.
The phrase “not fear, but its opposite: the excitement of being exactly where he was supposed to be” successfully subverts the reader’s expectation of anxiety.
The writer uses lots of techniques which makes the passage interesting and effective.
summaryParts.explain: This is too vague. Good language analysis names specific techniques, quotes precisely, and explains the particular effect created — not just that it’s ‘interesting.’

silver.quote: One girl in the front row was whispering to herself with her eyes shut, her lips moving fast as though reciting a prayer or a formula.
silver.context: A good response analyses specific language choices: “floor wax and adrenaline” (synaesthesia), the precise listing, the nervous physical actions (opening/closing hands, rolling necks), and the girl whispering “as though reciting a prayer or a formula” — this comparison blurs spiritual and intellectual preparation. Should explain how the language creates a charged, tense atmosphere.
silver.question: [Q2 skill] How does the writer use language to describe the atmosphere of the exam hall before the papers are turned over?

chips.text: Yusuf sees intellectual challenge as exciting, not frightening
The question is literally decorated with beautiful drawings
The word subverts the reader’s expectation — we expected fear, not joy
It reveals Yusuf’s passion for the subject
Yusuf is not taking the competition seriously
It marks the emotional turning point of the passage

silver.question: [Q2 skill] Yusuf sees the first question and thinks “It was beautiful.” What does this unexpected word choice reveal?

silver.quote: She told them to turn over their papers. Yusuf turned his over. The first question was one he had never seen before. It was beautiful.
silver.context: A good response analyses the structural arc: clinical setup (desk details) → nervous energy (competitors’ fidgeting) → authority figure (invigilator) → turning point (the question) → emotional resolution (excitement). Should note how the short sentence “It was beautiful” disrupts the tense rhythm and signals the shift. The ending is unexpected because the entire passage prepared the reader for anxiety, not joy.
silver.question: [Q3 skill] How does the writer structure this passage to create a shift from tension to excitement?
[Q2 skill] Highlight the phrase that most effectively conveys the invigilator’s authority.
silver.answer_text: her voice carried without effort to every corner of the room
silver.explanation: The phrase “without effort” suggests effortless command and authority. The voice reaching “every corner” implies she controls the entire space, reinforcing the formal, high-stakes atmosphere.

steps.content: The opening sentence combines a real smell (“floor wax”) with an abstract one (“adrenaline”). This is a form of synaesthesia that makes the tension feel physical and present in the room.

steps.label: Step 2
steps.content: The precise numbering (“Seventy-two desks,” “rows of eight”) creates a sense of rigid order. The listing of objects (“number card, two sharpened pencils, and a glass of water”) adds to the controlled, almost clinical atmosphere.

steps.label: Step 3
steps.content: The detail “nobody would drink” is telling — the water is there for a purpose no one will use it for, suggesting the formality is partly performative.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: The writer combines the real (“floor wax”) with the abstract (“adrenaline”) to make tension tangible. The precise numbering and listing of identical desk items create a clinical, regimented atmosphere. The detail that nobody will drink the water adds a quietly absurd note, suggesting the formal setup is more about ritual than function.

ai_marking_prompts.full_evaluation:
You are a GCSE English Language tutor. The student is writing a full critical evaluation. This is a high-value question. Mark their response using these levels:

- Mastering (excellent): Sustained, convincing evaluation with a clear thesis; multiple pieces of well-analysed evidence; considers how different techniques work together; may include counter-argument; personal and perceptive.
- Secure (good): Clear evaluative position with 2+ pieces of evidence; analysis of techniques and effects; personal engagement; mostly convincing.
- Developing (needs_work): Some evaluation but inconsistent; may alternate between evaluation and description; evidence used but analysis is surface-level.
- Emerging (not_valid): Describes or retells without evaluating; no personal position; no analysis of how techniques create effects.

Be encouraging. This is a 20-mark question skill — reward ambition and insight. Respond in JSON: {"quality":"excellent|good|needs_work|not_valid","feedback":"2-3 sentences","improvement":"optional brief tip"}
ai_marking_prompts.language_analysis:
You are a GCSE English Language tutor. The student is analysing how a writer uses language to create effects. Mark their response using these levels:

- Mastering (excellent): Identifies specific words/phrases and explains their connotations and effects precisely; considers how language creates mood, imagery, or attitude; uses quotation or close reference; perceptive.
- Secure (good): Identifies techniques or word choices and explains effects with some precision; evidence used; mostly convincing analysis.
- Developing (needs_work): Identifies some language features but explanation is vague; may feature-spot without analysing effect.
- Emerging (not_valid): Retells or paraphrases the text; no analysis of language; no reference to specific words or techniques.

Be encouraging. Reward genuine insight. Do NOT require PEE structure. Respond in JSON: {"quality":"excellent|good|needs_work|not_valid","feedback":"2-3 sentences","improvement":"optional brief tip"}
